title: TEACHER VOICE: Students are trained to answer questions, but they are rarely taught how to ask them
summary:

I told them I would not be grading their answers. I would be grading their questions. The reaction was immediate — and telling. […]

The post TEACHER VOICE: Students are trained to answer questions, but they are rarely taught how to ask them appeared first on The Hechinger Report.
full_text:
After weeks discussing the U.S. economy and the Federal Reserve’s monetary policy, I gave my students an unusual assignment: Act as financial journalists and prepare three questions for a senior Fed official.

I told them I would not be grading their answers.

I would be grading their questions.

The reaction was immediate — and telling. Students who were comfortable explaining concepts suddenly hesitated. Others leaned in, thinking more carefully than they had all semester. The exercise revealed something simple but unsettling: While students are trained to answer questions, they are rarely taught how to ask them.

In a world in which answers are increasingly easy to generate, the more important skill is knowing what to ask. Yet our education system is not designed to teach it.

If we are serious about preparing students for the future, we must rethink what we value. We must shift from teaching what to think, to teaching how to think — prioritizing curiosity, reasoning, judgment and the ability to engage with complexity. And we must place greater emphasis on questions.

For generations, education in the United States and elsewhere has followed a familiar model: Teachers deliver knowledge, students absorb it and success is measured by how accurately the students can reproduce it. Standardized tests reward precision. Grades reward correctness. The system rewards answers.

That model made sense when information was scarce.

But today, information is abundant — almost overwhelmingly so. With a smartphone, students can access more knowledge in seconds than previous generations could in years. Artificial intelligence (AI) can summarize, analyze and generate content almost instantly.

Yet our classrooms still operate as if access to information is the central challenge. It is not. The real challenge is making sense of it.

Related: Interested in innovations in higher education? Subscribe to our free biweekly higher education newsletter.

When information is scarce, education is about access. When information is abundant, it must be about discernment — about deciding what is reliable, what is relevant and what is worth attention.

But we continue to emphasize memorization over meaning and answers over inquiry.

In doing so, we risk producing students who are well-trained to respond but poorly equipped to think. The rise of AI has made this gap impossible to ignore.

Much of the concern around AI focuses on job loss. And it is true that routine tasks — both physical and cognitive — are increasingly automated. But this does not make human intelligence obsolete. It changes what kinds of intelligence matter.

Machines excel at processing information, identifying patterns and executing well-defined tasks. But processing information is not the same as exercising human judgment — especially when problems involve context, ambiguity, ethics and creativity.

In other words, the more capable our machines become, the more valuable human skills become.

Among those skills is the ability to ask meaningful questions. AI, of course, can generate answers in seconds. But the quality and usefulness of those answers depend greatly on the questions and instructions given. A vague question produces a vague answer. A thoughtful question produces insight.

The tool does not define the problem. We do. Yet from elementary school through college, students are assessed on how well they answer questions posed by others.

The questions are structured. The parameters are clear. The solutions are known. But the real world does not present problems this way.

It presents challenges that are messy, evolving and often poorly defined. Before solving them, one must first determine what the question actually is.

And that is precisely what we are not teaching. We are preparing students for a world of answers while they are entering a world of questions.

That classroom experience stayed with me. My students had spent weeks learning about the economy and monetary policy. Yet when asked to move beyond answering questions to framing their own, many struggled.

That is the challenge before us. The United States has long prided itself on innovation. But innovation does not come from a system that effectively discourages questioning. It comes from one that cultivates it.

Related: OPINION: Knowing how to use AI tools is not the same as knowing how to apply them responsibly. Colleges must do more

We now face a choice.

We can continue refining an education system designed for a different era — one that rewards correct answers. Or we can build one that prepares students for a world defined by uncertainty, complexity and constant change.

That world will not reward those who simply know. It will reward those who can think. And thinking begins not with answers — but with better questions.

Hiranya K. Nath is Distinguished Professor of Economics at Sam Houston State University. He has taught economics at the university level for more than two decades. The views expressed are his own.

Contact the opinion editor at opinion@hechingerreport.org.

full_text:
A magistrate who told a court user “I want to slap you around a bit, too” has come under fire for her offensive and inappropriate language.

The remark was one of several made by Victorian magistrate Vicky Prapas that the state’s judicial watchdog has found to be inappropriate.

Others included asking someone in court: “Do you reckon the substance is screwing with the way you’re thinking?” and asserting that another person “believes their own bullshit”.

The latter comment was made in the presence of a school group, the judicial commission of Victoria said in its findings last week.

The watchdog opened the investigation after receiving a complaint from Victoria Legal Aid concerning Prapas’ rotation through a Melbourne drug court.

The investigation substantiated a range of allegations, including that the magistrate made threatening or intimidating remarks to legal practitioners when they proposed to make or support complaints against her.

Those comments amounted to a “pattern of victimisation”, the commission found.

Prapas was also found to have made an offensive comment about a person from a marginalised group and made an unprofessional remark about another member of the judiciary.

In the written decision, Prapas acknowledged, among other things, that her conduct in some instances had been “unfiltered and intemperate” and that she would have expressed herself differently with the benefit of hindsight.

But she referred to the unique jurisdiction of a drug court, including that her intention was to promote participant recovery, accountability and community safety within its therapeutic framework.

She said she had reflected carefully on the matters raised, and had taken steps to ensure that her communication remained effective, respectful and less susceptible to misunderstanding.

The watchdog was unable to substantiate some allegations, including that the magistrate demonstrated cultural insensitivity.

In handing down its findings, the commission acknowledged drug court proceedings can warrant “open and frank” discussions.

“However, these features do not displace a judicial officer’s obligation to afford all court users civility and respect,” it said.

The brunt of the complaint was referred to the chief magistrate, Lisa Hannan, with recommendations she counsel Prapas.

The watchdog also recommended Prapas familiarise herself with the commission’s conduct guidelines and attend an educational event within a year.

title: A curmudgeon’s guide to the 2026 US elections | Dave Schilling
summary:
From the cheesecake factory discourse to the double Dan Sullivans, campaign season has been ridiculous

Chances are, as you’re reading this, your bunker is fully stocked, your doors are locked, and you’re peeking at your computer screen through gaps between your fingers.

After all, it’s election day on Tuesday. Once again, democracy will be tested – like Beavis & Butthead taking the SATs. I’m not looking forward to it, and I’m sure you aren’t either.

Dave Schilling is a Los Angeles-based writer and humorist

Continue reading...
full_text:
Chances are, as you’re reading this, your bunker is fully stocked, your doors are locked, and you’re peeking at your computer screen through gaps between your fingers.

After all, it’s election day on Tuesday. Once again, democracy will be tested – like Beavis & Butthead taking the SATs. I’m not looking forward to it, and I’m sure you aren’t either.

I’m old enough to remember when American elections, and especially the once-sleepy midterms, were a placid affair that anyone with a calculator and a friend at the Associated Press could predict.

Now, it feels like anything can and will happen this week – from delayed results and slow counts to Donald Trump sending in the DC Comics Suicide Squad to your local polling place. That’s all we need, John Cena checking your ID before you vote.

It’s enough to make you crawl up into a ball and beg for mommy. But fear is a passive emotion, one that leaves a person paralyzed and incapable of action.

My preference is for the fully formed anger of the middle-aged curmudgeon. A shaken fist and a choice expletive is healthier than babbling for hours in your panic room. So, in lieu of a voter guide telling you how to fill out your ballot, here’s a list of all the most irritating, confounding and downright stupid things to scream about on Tuesday.

The Cheesecake Factory discourse

During a recent campaign stop, the former president Barack Obama compared the aesthetics of the recent Trump-led White House renovations with a Cheesecake Factory. Not only am I annoyed that this is even a talking point during a crucial campaign, I also resent the comparison being made. I’d rather eat at a Cheesecake Factory than the White House, any day of the week. I have to assume Bill Maher agrees with me.

The continued importance of Spencer Pratt

Here in California, the race everyone is talking about is a contest for Los Angeles mayor, a famous stepping stone to jobs as prestigious as “Ambassador to Country Chosen by Random Lottery Draw” or “Special Adviser to Herbalife”. It’s neck-and-neck between incumbent Karen Bass and the city councilperson Nithya Raman. The unfortunate twist in this daytime soap opera is that the reality show star they combined to defeat in the first round of voting this summer, Spencer Pratt, is still popular enough that his supporters could tip the scales toward one candidate or the other. The only thing I can think of that’s worse than Spencer Pratt as mayor of LA is Spencer Pratt deciding the next mayor of LA.

The curious case of the two Dan Sullivans

According to the New York Times, some Democrats figured out that the best way to unseat the senator Dan Sullivan was to force him to run against himself. Retired teacher Dan Sullivan was allegedly recruited to run for US Senate by the campaign of Democrat Mary Peltola, in the hopes of unseating … Dan Sullivan. (The Peltola campaign has denied any involvement in his candidacy.)

The Sullivan v Sullivan smackdown has the Republican party so worried that the justice department is suing to invalidate the results of the election if Sullivan (the senator) narrowly loses to Sullivan (the not-senator) or Peltola (the not-Sullivan).

I’m no fan of Dan Sullivan, but I’m not sure how I feel about Dan Sullivan either! This is the kind of goofy dirty trick that makes people hate politics. Who are you really fooling here? Old people? People who are too busy to read the fine print about which Dan Sullivan is the incumbent Alaskan senator? People with an acute case of Sullivantitis (a crippling disease that causes blindness to the name “Dan Sullivan”)? Can’t this country ever be normal?

Please don’t message me. I realize the answer is no. I just hope this election is more entertaining than The Undertaker v The Undertaker at WWF SummerSlam 1994. Unlike that match, this face-off of doppelgangers won’t involve Leslie Nielsen.

The continued push to close polling places

In an attempt to depress turnout amongst Democratic-leaning voters, red state election boards in states such as North Carolina are shutting polling places in blue areas. In North Carolina in particular, voting sites were shut on numerous college campuses, but that didn’t stop a group of predominantly students from organizing marches in excess of two hours so that they could maintain the franchise.

When I was a young man, the main tool crooked politicians had to keep people from voting was good, old-fashioned apathy. We should have changed the motto on the quarter from “E pluribus unum” to “They’re all bums, anyway.” In 2026, politicians have infuriated people to such a degree that they’ll walk miles just to vote.

It’s inspiring to see young people exercising their rights in the face of an actively hostile state government, but I find the notion of our nation’s leaders blatantly making it more onerous for citizens to vote absolutely abhorrent. I mean, the peer pressure is bad enough.

‘I voted’ stickers and selfies

I get why the stickers exist. An elaborate campaign of shame and embarrassment for those that didn’t bother to vote. I can’t think of two more powerful forces in my life than shame and embarrassment. They’re really the only two reasons I get out of bed these days, but I don’t have to like it.

Like a lollipop at the end of a haircut, the “I voted” sticker is the little treat at the end of a long period of interminable waiting. The only difference is, I don’t need to take a picture with my root beer-flavored Dum Dum. And I hate to be cynical here, but anyone who hasn’t planned on or even considered voting will not be swayed by a sticker.

As much as I despise people shirking their responsibility to democracy, I hate internet trends even more. Instead of wearing an “I voted” sticker on Tuesday, just slap it on your laptop. That way, anyone in your general vicinity will have to stop and double-check that there isn’t an election that day.

Donald Trump’s Mr America beauty pageant

This is Donald Trump’s last campaign of his risible political career. He has been a cancerous influence on our discourse since 2011, breaking traditions, norms, rules, and some priceless artifacts along the way.

I’m sure he’s getting nostalgic for the rush of election fervor – the ups and downs, the thrill of victory and the agony of not admitting defeat. These are some of the last campaign rallies he’ll ever lead, some of the final moments of political combat he’ll engage in in his lifetime.

Most of us would get wistful, maybe a tad somber. These days will never come again. Instead, the president is pondering the strength and power that emanates from various Republican buttocks.

Nothing, and I mean nothing, makes me bang my head against a wall this election cycle than my social media feed being littered with clips of Donald Trump sexualizing his colleagues.

title: US midterms: What to know about independent voters and candidates
summary: Despite a record number of independents, third-party candidates and voters struggle to penetrate the two-party system.
full_text:
As Americans head to the polls on Tuesday in the much-anticipated midterms, the record number of voters identifying as independent could prove decisive for control of the US Congress and state legislatures.

Nearly half of US voters – as many as 117 million adults – now identify as politically independent, with the two major parties, Democrats and Republicans, jockeying for their votes.

list 3 of 4How will the Iran war shape the outcome of the US midterm vote?

list 4 of 4Why did Democrat Haley Stevens just endorse a Republican for US Senate?

end of list

At the same time, independent or third-party candidates win few federal or state seats. The Democratic and Republican parties have dominated US politics, from state legislatures to the US Congress and the presidency, for generations.

“The whole [electoral] system is built to frustrate the independence of voters,” says Rick Bennett, the former Republican Party chair in Maine, where he is running to become only the third independent governor in the state’s history.

Bennett’s candidacy runs headlong into one of the most stubborn contradictions in US politics: While millions of eligible voters reject Republican and Democratic labels, far fewer will cast their ballots for independent candidates.

“For decades, candidates outside the Democratic and Republican parties have struggled to achieve [a high] level of support,” political scientist AJ Simmons said. “[But] 2026 is shaping up to be one of the strongest election cycles for independent candidates in recent memory.”

Who are independents and how will they vote?

According to the Pew Research Center’s annual National Public Opinion Reference Survey, 44 percent of US adults identify as politically independent. This is in contrast to 29 percent who identify as Democrat and 28 percent as Republican.

But there is a caveat: Most self-described independents still gravitate towards one of the major parties. Independents who express absolutely no partisan leaning make up only about 7-10 percent of the total electorate.

These “true” independents are sought after by candidates because they are persuadable, the core of the coveted so-called swing vote in a deeply divided and partisan electorate and political system.

In the 2026 midterm elections, 52 percent of likely independent voters are supporting Democrats, while 39 percent back Republicans, polling firm Marist suggests.

Frustration with President Donald Trump is permeating the midterm electoral landscape, with independent respondents more than three times as likely to say their vote is mainly against the president, and 28 percent saying they are voting for “change”.

Why does the US have a two-party system?

The US does not legally restrict elections to two parties, and many local officials are not party-affiliated.

But for more powerful federal and statewide seats like Tuesday’s House of Representatives and Senate races, the winner-take-all electoral system and single-member congressional districts work against outsiders and can discourage voters from backing them.

Even substantial support for a minor party is rarely concentrated enough in one district to win a congressional seat.

Voters, too, can unknowingly reinforce the system.

Polling trends and data further suggest that voters who identify as or prefer an independent will often instead back a Republican or Democrat they see as more politically viable. Voters are also reluctant to support “spoilers”, who may peel away votes from one of the two major-party candidates.

Why do third parties struggle to win US elections?

Bernard Tamas, a political scientist at Valdosta State University who studies third parties, said that although laws are often blamed for keeping third-party candidates off the ballot, “there is very little evidence that legal barriers are undermining these candidates”.

The real barrier, he says, is money.

A total of $14.8bn was spent on federal elections during the 2024 presidential cycle, and the 2026 midterms are projected to surpass that, reaching up to $11.6bn in political advertisement spending alone.

The Democratic National Committee (DNC), which heads the Democratic Party, raised nearly $252.3m during the 2026 midterm campaign cycle while the Republican National Committee (RNC) took in about $341m.

Unlike other democracies, the US “offers virtually no public support” or funding to political parties and does not set limits on campaign spending”, Tamas said. Independent candidates “raise very little money” and are less well known by voters.

Why don’t more Americans vote independent?

Lesley Shedd, a Republican strategist, told Al Jazeera that the surge in voters identifying as independents obscures their support for one of the two major parties.

“When somebody says they are independent, they really are a Republican or Democrat but they maybe don’t agree with the party on absolutely every issue,” Shedd said. “Or they [just] don’t want to feel as though they are part of the culture of the swamp of [Washington] DC.”

The real test for independent candidates is persuading Americans to vote for them, not just a “protest vote” against the system. And voters are reluctant to cast a “wasted” ballot, Simmons said, given the most competitive candidates are Democrats or Republicans.

There are efforts to support independent candidates. The Independent Leadership Council, launched in July by former Democrat-turned-independent Senator Joe Manchin, provides donors and campaign resources for independent congressional candidates. The project has raised more than $10m.

But the longer-term test, analysts maintain, is whether independent candidates can be viable across multiple races and election cycles.

There is currently one independent in the US House and two in the US Senate. None holds a state governor seat.

Bennett, the independent Maine candidate, is one of just 11 independent or third-party candidates vying for gubernatorial or US Senate seats whom Simmons expects to surpass the 5 percent vote threshold often used to gauge electoral viability.

Additionally, Simmons sees several ways independent congressional hopefuls could throw the midterm map into disarray, mainly in two key states: Nebraska and Montana.

He identified Nebraska’s independent Senate candidate Dan Osborn, a 51-year-old Navy veteran, as the “most likely alternative candidate to win” across the country, given the race has been deemed a toss-up by RealClearPolling, an election analysis website.

The Nebraska Democratic Party chose not to field a replacement nominee after its candidate withdrew, leaving Osborn as the principal challenger to Republican Pete Ricketts.

In Montana, Simmons sees another opening for an independent, though the race is complicated by the possibility of an unpredictable “spoiler” effect.

Seth Bodnar, a former University of Montana president and Army veteran, is running against Republican Kurt Alme for the US Senate seat. He is being backed by the Independent Leadership Council, which is also supporting California Congressman Kevin Kiley, who left the Republican Party to seek re-election as an independent.

Democratic US Senate candidate Alani Bankhead could siphon off support from the same centre-left and anti-Republican pool of voters that Bodnar draws from, risking a three-way vote and potentially leaving the Republican to collect the spoils.

“Montana is the second most likely,” Simmons said, adding that “if that were to happen, the Republican Party would be having an extraordinarily bad night”.

In Idaho and South Dakota, independent candidates are not forecast to win, but they are expected to make Republicans pay for treating those seats as safe, diverting money, campaign time and attention to races Republicans may have otherwise taken for granted.

The greatest impact of independents may be the pressure they have historically brought to bear on the major parties to “implement a new policy or govern more effectively”, Simmons said.

title: ‘Being to Learn’ Rather Than ‘Learning to Be’: Shifting Thinking About Authentic Assessment
summary:
Emerging from tensions created by theory–practice gap rhetoric, authentic assessment has been heralded as a pedagogical vaccine. Now firmly embedded in the vernacular of higher education, authentic assessment offers learning designers a rich pool of innovative possibilities. These approaches have been shown to boost student engagement while offering academics a defense of the relevance of […]

The post ‘Being to Learn’ Rather Than ‘Learning to Be’: Shifting Thinking About Authentic Assessment appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
Emerging from tensions created by theory–practice gap rhetoric, authentic assessment has been heralded as a pedagogical vaccine. Now firmly embedded in the vernacular of higher education, authentic assessment offers learning designers a rich pool of innovative possibilities. These approaches have been shown to boost student engagement while offering academics a defense of the relevance of their assessment designs. At its core, authentic assessment involves designing tasks that mirror real-world challenges, helping students develop the knowledge and skills they’ll need beyond graduation. We usually find such tasks embedded within existing curricula and programs, as common fixtures of what we describe here as the ‘learning to be’ paradigm; the process of helping students acquire the knowledge and skills of a profession.

However, regardless of how novel an authentic assessment may be, while it remains a feature of traditional university systems thinking, it may contribute to the same divide it seeks to bridge. Central to this dilemma is the argument that the issue lies not in the quality of innovation, but in the divergent objectives and priorities of the modern campus and the workplace. Put simply, it is not the tool but the context in which it is used. While ‘learning to be’ approaches emphasise knowledge and skills acquisition, they often overlook the attributes and qualities most valued by employers.

To illustrate this disconnect, consider the following industry priorities.

Discrete Sample of Knowledge or Skills

Authentic assessment captures insights into students’ optimized efforts at a single time point, typically reflecting content knowledge or specific skills. In contrast, workplaces value consistency, reliability, and personal attributes, where a worker’s weakest area may shape perceptions of their competence.

Attendance and Punctuality

Academic staff increasingly contend with low student attendance, with flexible learning measures accommodating participation on students’ terms. In contrast, the professional world is far less forgiving, where punctuality and reliability are non-negotiable.

Work Deadlines

Many academics now anticipate a surge of extension requests as due dates approach. Institutional policies often allow automated approvals to support student success. Conversely, workplaces depend on work being delivered on time and within budget, with employees held accountable.

Direction vs. Initiative

Employers value initiative and self-directed action. Yet, when authentic assessments remain highly prescriptive, students may become passive, awaiting instruction rather than demonstrating independence.

Engaging with Critical Feedback and Grade Appeals

Employers expect individuals to respect expertise and respond constructively to feedback. In contrast, students may challenge or negotiate grades, exposing authentic assessments to cultural inconsistencies.

Narrow Scope and Censored Feedback

Assessment workloads and the need for defensible grading often lead to standardized responses. While transparent, these may restrict nuanced feedback and shield students from the candid critiques encountered in professional practice.

Student Comfort Zones

Students often control where they sit, who they work with, and how tasks are completed. In professional settings, individuals must adapt to unfamiliar colleagues and environments.

It is argued that solutions to these disparities reside in the coexistence of higher education and industry cultures, supported by an elevated awareness of expectations. This requires subtle shifts within authentic assessment philosophy.

The “Being to Learn” Philosophy

One solution lies in a fundamental shift in pedagogical thinking—moving beyond what students need to learn or do to consider who they need to become and how they must act. This is not a call to withdraw essential supports, but an invitation to infuse professional expectations throughout the student journey. If universities are to bridge education and employment, they must illuminate the often-unspoken norms of professional life and provide opportunities for students to develop them.

The “Being to Learn” approach recognises that professional identity formation requires immersive, sustained support beyond a single embedded task. It reflects an intentional effort to design experiences that engage students in the how of working, not just the what.

Below are suggestions that embody this philosophy:

Clearly Describe Future Work

Frame assessments beyond content, incorporating professional contexts such as shift work, remote practice, client expectations, and role demands.

Refer to the Rule Book

Use standards from professional bodies and regulators to anchor authentic assessment design.

Real Assessment Demands Real Feedback

Provide candid, meaningful feedback aligned with workplace expectations.

Highlight Attendance and Punctuality

Encourage reflection on the professional consequences of lateness or absence.

Encourage Experimentation

Design tasks that require initiative, innovation, and independent problem-solving.

Speak the Language

Introduce disciplinary terminology to support professional identity formation.

Promote a Classroom Code of Conduct

Encourage professional behaviours, collaboration, and respectful engagement.

Embrace Discomfort

Rotate groups and require students to work with unfamiliar peers to build adaptability.

Authentic assessment has enhanced the relevance of higher education assessment practices, but it is not a silver bullet. To truly prepare students for life beyond university, we must shift from preparing them to complete tasks to helping them become professionals. The “Being to Learn” philosophy offers a powerful next step by bridging learning, identity, and action in pursuit of meaningful and enduring educational outcomes.

Dr. James Thompson is a senior lecturer in the School of Pharmacy and Biomedical Science at Adelaide University in South Australia. For several decades he has been a champion for advancing the assessment practices and decision making about the competency and the work-readiness of graduates across health disciplines. He has contributed original theory and insights which have been broadly adopted in the practice of others.

title: Foley Catheters and First-Year Composition: Implementing High-Impact Practices through Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration
summary:

The post Foley Catheters and First-Year Composition: Implementing High-Impact Practices through Cross-Disciplinary Collaboration appeared first on Faculty Focus | Higher Ed Teaching & Learning.
full_text:
According to the Association of American Colleges and Universities, active learning is an essential part of a modern college education. High Impact Practices (HIPs) use collaborative and active learning strategies to improve student engagements and outcomes. White (2018) explained that while HIPs can positively impact student success, budgetary restraints can present challenges to implementation. Therefore, faculty are finding ways to create active learning experiences without a high cost to institutions.

Cross-disciplinary collaboration presents an opportunity to use HIPs to engage students in the core curriculum. In my case, the First-Year Writing (FYW) classroom offers a unique setting to use HIPs to build on how writing creates common spaces not only in FYW, but also expands those spaces into discipline-specific areas, such as nursing. Cross-disciplinary collaboration through FYW not only provides students with an early look at their majors but also teaches them how to decompartmentalize the writing skills they learn in FYW and apply them to a broader experience.

This article will focus on one such collaboration between English (English 1101) and Nursing and the impact of cross-disciplinary activities and HIPs on students in a discipline-specific FYW course.

Importance of Collaboration

Collaborative projects can provide students with deeper learning experiences and opportunities for increasing communication (written and oral) skills both inside the classroom and within the community (White, 2018; Bresciani, 2015). The FYW classroom provides a unique setting to build on momentum in cases where students are unable to have an early introduction to their major. FYW challenges students to understand the connection of strong writing to their majors, especially if the material in the course correlates to relevant subject matter in the major. The goal in creating this cost-effective nursing-specific English 1101 was to ask students to think specifically about how writing relates to a more universal experience (medical professions) in order to express the importance of humanities beyond the composition classroom.

Collaboration, particularly in course design and implementation, can often seem like a heavy lift. In some cases, faculty can be protective of course material and design, and in others, challenges exist in finding partnerships outside of specific disciplinary departments. In the following, I hope to show how this type of critical work can happen organically and effectively while bringing satisfaction and appreciation not only to students but to the faculty involved.

Process of Implementation

Over the course of a semester and over the summer, I worked with a nursing faculty member to refine the necessary concepts for bringing the course into the classroom. I started with the basic course learning outcomes for our institution’s English 1101.

From there, I and my nursing faculty partner, explored what concepts would be important for students interested in the nursing program to learn early in their academic careers. I began with highlighting the connection between the humanities and health care through learning about and constructing a medical narrative where students had to articulate their interest in pursuing a nursing career. Then, I focused on the importance of communication in relaying critical information through instructions by creating a process project, which included a demonstration (by my nursing partner) of a Foley catheter insertion using a medical mannequin, followed by a hands-on opportunity for students to practice this foundational healthcare procedure. Finally, I had students hone their research skills by exploring relevant and current healthcare-related issues and presenting them in a multimedia assignment. Instead of MLA, as is common in most humanities courses, students used APA formatting and citations throughout the course to better prepare them for the nursing program.

Please scan the QR code below for copies of the assignments.

Lessons Learned and Advice

Engagement

Students were more motivated to engage with assignments. They appreciated exposure to nursing concepts early in their academic careers and enjoyed forming an early relationship with a nursing faculty member. The course sparked their intellectual curiosity and got them thinking about the deeper issues within their major and future profession. When learning is decompartmentalized, students can see connection between academic and life experiences. Potential nursing students expressed excitement for discipline-specific core classes and, sometimes, students realized that the hands-on activities showed them that nursing was not their best fit, well before they spent years working towards acceptance into the nursing program.

Collaboration

Collaboration opportunities don’t have to be complicated, expensive, or overly time-consuming. Simple conversations and activities can be cost-effective while academically sound and engaging. Partnerships can happen in surprising situations. The nursing English 1101 collaboration started as a kernel of an idea while riding in the back of a college-issued Ford Taurus on the way home from a teaching and learning conference. It’s important to note that collaborative course work should involve immediate supervisors (chairs and deans), advisors, and the Registrar. In my situation, we needed to make sure the course was populated with future nursing students, which would be information the Registrar provided and advisors actively used for registration.

Final Thoughts

This collaboration provided students a way into a conversation about their major before they spent two years of preparation getting into their major courses. Unlike many other majors, nursing students do not take any nursing courses until they are accepted into the program, at least two years into their college education. For many, junior-level nursing courses are their first exposure to nursing concepts and conversations. A collaboration like the one I have presented allows an early look at disciplinary concepts and presents students with a stronger understanding of their educational decisions and career choices. Team teaching collaborative options and knowledge sharing that rely on HIPs, such as hands-on, experiential activities, can be designed to support strong communication skills and give students a concrete and vibrant support system that allows for intellectual curiosity and advanced critical thinking.

Dr. Stephanie B. Conner is a tenured associate professor of English with a focus on composition and Interdisciplinary Studies at the College of Coastal Georgia with over 25 years of experience. She has presented at nearly 40 conferences including the Conference on College Composition and Communication and published her work in journals such as Response to Writing. Her research is grounded in pedagogical best practices in college writing instruction as well as professional development in teaching and learning. Her most recent work includes a collaborative, dual-institution IRB-approved study with three other composition professors exploring faculty emotional responses to plagiarism and AI in writing courses and is due for publication at Composition Forum in spring 2026. Other research areas include incorporating Writing Center coaches into peer review activities and using weak examples as instructional material to bolster students’ critical thinking about citation and AI use. Dr. Conner has also worked collaboratively to develop a discipline-specific first-year writing course for students interested in the nursing program.

title: Montag: Spyware-Warnung für Bundespolitiker, Meta mit eigenem humanoiden Roboter
summary: Angriffe auf Politiker-iPhones + Meta-Roboter für Haushaltsaufgaben + Sam Altmans Idee gegen Speicherkrise + Internetsteuer Frankreichs + Folgen der Zollreform
full_text:
Müssen sich Bundespolitiker Sorgen machen, dass sich auf ihren iPhones Schadsoftware befindet? Der Digitalminister bestätigt einen amtlichen Hinweis. Demnach hat Apple vor der Kompromittierung bestimmter Geräte mit Spyware gewarnt. Derweil soll Meta Platforms mit Unterstützung des chinesischen Start-ups Fourier Roboter in Menschengestalt entwickelt haben. Damit wolle der Konzern die eigenen KI-Agenten auf Haushaltsaufgaben trainieren. Ein Verkauf dieser Roboter auf Nvidia-Basis ist nicht geplant. Durch KI-Nutzung wie diese steigen die Speicherpreise weiter rasant, eine schnelle Lösung gibt es nicht – außer alles KI-Rechenzentren zu überlassen, findet Sam Altman. Lokale KI-Modelle seien eine Verschwendung von Ressourcen, RAM würde in der Cloud besser genutzt – die wichtigsten Meldungen im kurzen Überblick.

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Das Bundesamt für Sicherheit in der Informationstechnik (BSI) hat Bundestagsabgeordnete und Regierungsmitglieder laut ARD-Hauptstadtstudio vor einem möglichen Angriff mit Spähsoftware auf Handys gewarnt. Bei dem Hinweis gehe es um eine Bedrohungsbenachrichtigung für iPhones von Apple. Die Geräte hätten seit dem 29. Oktober eine Warnung erhalten, wonach Apple einen Angriff mit sogenannter Mercenary-Spyware erkannt habe. Digitalminister Karsten Wildberger (CDU) sagte dazu, es gebe „eine Meldung von Apple, dass bestimmte Geräte gegebenenfalls kompromittiert wurden mit sogenannter Spyware“. Das BSI habe „superschnell reagiert“ und alle Betroffenen angeschrieben, was in diesem Fall zu tun sei. Offen ist bislang, „um was es sich hier konkret handelt“: Apple meldet Kompromittierung von Geräten durch Spyware.

Meta Platforms hat gemeinsam mit dem chinesischen Robotik-Start-up Fourier Prototypen eines humanoiden Roboters entwickelt. Der 'Max' genannte Roboter soll Menschen bei alltäglichen Aufgaben im Haushalt unterstützen können, wird jetzt berichtet. Der Prototyp von Max wiegt etwa 48 Kilogramm, ist ungefähr 1,5 Meter groß und besitzt demnach einen Bildschirm im Kopf, um Gesichtsausdrücke darstellen zu können, fünf Lautsprecher und Hände mit fünf Fingern, die für den Umgang mit kleinen Objekten entwickelt wurden. Damit will der Facebook-Konzern die eigenen KI-Modelle auf Alltagsaufgaben erweitern. Auf Nachfrage streitet Meta die Arbeit an Robotern nicht ab, aber es handelt sich um ein internes Projekt. Die Roboter sollen nicht in den Verkauf gelangen: Meta arbeitet offenbar mit chinesischer Hilfe an humanoidem Haushaltsroboter.

Der ständig fortschreitende Bau von neuen Rechenzentren für Künstliche Intelligenz und der damit einhergehende Bedarf nach Halbleitern aller Art, insbesondere Arbeitsspeicher (DRAM), hat seit über einem Jahr zu einer Vervielfachung der Preise am Markt für Endkunden geführt. Die Chiphersteller eilen von einem Rekordgewinn zum anderen, und das soll auch mindestens im kommenden Jahr noch anhalten. Als einer der Hauptverantwortlichen dafür gilt OpenAI mit seinem Mitgründer Sam Altman, deren KI Rechenzentren mit enormen Kapazitäten und Speicher erfordert. Dass sich manche Nutzer inzwischen auf lokale KI-Modelle, statt die Lösungen in der Cloud verlassen, trägt nach Altmans Meinung zur Verschärfung der Situation bei. Denn dieser Speicher würde „nur 5 Prozent der Zeit tatsächlich genutzt“: OpenAI-Chef Sam Altman findet DRAM in Privathand „schrecklich“.

Content-Anbieter im Internet sollen künftig eine Abgabe für die Datenmenge entrichten, die sie über das Netz an französische Endnutzer ausliefern. Ein entsprechender Antrag der französischen Sozialisten in Frankreichs Nationalversammlung sorgt gerade für Diskussionen. Die Idee hinter der geplanten neuen Steuer: Unternehmen, die auf ihren Servern Inhalte anbieten, die Nutzer über das französische Web abrufen können, sollen künftig dafür zahlen. Und zwar 5,5 Cent pro Gigabyte, das an französische Endnutzer fließt. Den Großteil dieser Steuer sollen große Tech-Unternehmen wie Google, Meta, Amazon und Netflix zahlen, die laut der PS einen erheblichen Anteil am französischen Datenverkehr haben. Der Antrag macht aber keine Unterscheidung nach der Größe eines Unternehmens: Frankreich plant Internetsteuer von 5,5 Cent pro Gigabyte.

Zum Monatswechsel tritt mit der „Universellen Bearbeitungsgebühr“ (Universal Handling Fee, UHF) eine weitere Gebühr bei Bestellungen aus dem Nicht-EU-Ausland in Kraft. Zwei Euro müssen Anbieter dann für jede Warenposition einer Bestellung entrichten, die im Fernverkauf im Sinne der Zollverordnung direkt zu den Kunden auf den Weg gebracht wird. Zum direkten Weg zählt auch die Lieferung an einen Abholort. Das eindeutige Ziel der Übung: die enorme Paketflut aus Fernost weiter eindämmen. Mit der neuen Gebühr verteuern sich vor allem Kleinstimporte und gemischte Warensendungen. Offen ist jedoch, ob die Versandhändler die Gebühren über den Preis teilweise oder vollständig an die Nutzer weitergeben werden und somit das Geschäft der globalen massenhaften Kleinstwarensendungen zusammenbricht: Neue Zollgebühren pro Position, nicht pro Paket.

Auch noch wichtig:

Weiterlesen nach der Anzeige

Maus nach vorn, Blick nach unten: Manche steuern Ego-Shooter wie ein Flugzeug. Doch die Gen Z lacht sich darüber kaputt, heißt es im Missing Link: Invertierte Maussteuerung – sind die 1990er schuld?

Google experimentiert mit KI-Beschleunigern im Orbit. Jetzt lieferte das Projekt erste Daten: Erste Daten von Googles KI-Satellit.

Apples neue Funktionen „Live Rewind“ und „Siri Recap“ könnten unter US-Bundesstaatengesetze gegen das Abhören fallen. Rechtsgelehrte warnen, dies sei möglicherweise strafbar: US-Anwälte zu „Audio Intelligence“ auf der Apple Watch.

Das Projekt ArtCraft entstand per Vibe-Coding und ahmt Photoshop, PowerPoint & Co. nach. Wir diskutieren, was KI-Kopien können – und was nicht – im c't uplink zu Adobe-Konkurrenz: Das taugt KI-Klon PhotoCraft.

Eine Domainsperre sorgt beim RIPE-Treffen für Diskussionen. Wie können sich Betreiber gegen erratische US-Sanktionen wappnen? RIPE-Mitglieder diskutieren über Abhängigkeit von US-Internetinfrastruktur.

Die nordkoreanische Gruppe TraderTraitor ist für den milliardenschweren Hackerangriff auf Binance verantwortlich, sagt das FBI: Nordkorea steckt hinter Milliarden-Kryptodiebstahl bei Binance.

Auch wenn es auf den ersten Blick nicht so aussieht: Apple überholt das MacBook Pro kräftig. Hier eine Anzahl interessanter Neuerungen beim neuen MacBook Pro: Was sonst noch wichtig ist.

Mammutpanzer, Tesla-Spulen und alternative Weltgeschichte: „Command & Conquer: Alarmstufe Rot“ wird 30 Jahre alt. Warum der C&C-Nachfolger bis heute Kult ist: „Alarmstufe Rot“ wird 30.

Ein 2,5-stündiges Webinar zeigt detailliert, wie Entwickler und Betreiber älterer PHP-Anwendungen und -Websites sicher auf eine aktuelle PHP-Version upgraden: Vom Notfall-Patch nach PHP2Shell zum sicheren Upgrade.

Power-Mosfets aus Schleswig-Holstein werden künftig auf größeren Siliziumscheiben gefertigt – Vishay erweitert seine Chipfabrik: Förderung für 300mm-Wafer in Itzehoe an Vishay übergeben.

Waren von Shein, Temu oder AliExpress sind in der EU beliebt. Nun wird für die Einfuhr von Produkten eine neue Gebühr fällig. Was das für Verbraucher bedeutet, klärt unsere FAQ: Warum es neue Gebühren für Importe gibt, und was sie bringen sollen.
